Instead, it identifies categories of devices/services that are not covered.

## Specifically not covered under Policy 5B
NC Medicaid does **not** cover:

- **Devices for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience**, or for the convenience of the caregiver
- **Backup or duplicate devices** kept on hand or available at different locations
- **Devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities**
- **Devices or supplies covered by another agency**
- **Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care**, as defined in the policy’s care-coordination section  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics, § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment))

The policy also says coverage is denied when:

- the beneficiary does not meet **eligibility requirements** in Section 2.0,
- the beneficiary does not meet the **coverage criteria** in Section 3.0,
- the item/service **duplicates another provider’s** procedure, product, or service, or
- the item/service is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics, § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment))

## General criteria that must be met for coverage
For coverage under Policy 5B, the orthotic or prosthetic item/service must meet the general criteria in Section 3.1:

- It must be **individualized and specific** to the beneficiary
- It must be **consistent with the symptoms or confirmed diagnosis**
- It must **not exceed the beneficiary’s needs**
- It must be able to be **safely furnished**
- There must be **no equally effective, more conservative, or less costly treatment available statewide**
- It must **not be furnished primarily for convenience** of the beneficiary, caregiver, or provider  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics, § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment))

## Additional specific coverage criteria
Policy 5B also requires that orthotics/prosthetics:

- be **ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**
- be **medically necessary** to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level
- be **appropriate for use in a noninstitutional setting** where normal life activities occur
- be supported by a **face-to-face encounter** with the ordering clinician no more than **6 months before initiation**
- have the beneficiary’s need **reviewed at least annually**
- be a **reasonable and medically necessary part of the treatment plan**
- be **consistent with the diagnosis and medical condition**
- be of **high quality**, with replacement parts available
- be furnished by an appropriately enrolled, qualified provider  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics, § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment))

## Bottom line
The main “not covered” DME-type exclusions under the Orthotics & Prosthetics policy are **comfort/convenience items, backup/duplicate devices, items for nursing-facility residents, items covered by another agency, and equipment/supplies for hospice beneficiaries**. Coverage generally requires that the item be **medically necessary, individualized, ordered by an authorized clinician, non-duplicative, non-experimental, safe, and not primarily for convenience**.

per_question.question: What are the entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria for outpatient behavioral health services in NC Medicaid?

One caveat: the tool’s full-text return for the continued service section appears truncated at the end of the last bullet, so I can quote what it clearly provides, but I can’t verify any missing words beyond that cutoff from the retrieved text.## NC Medicaid outpatient behavioral health criteria

For **outpatient behavioral health services provided by direct-enrolled providers**, NC Medicaid sets the criteria in **Clinical Coverage Policy 8C**, effective **April 15, 2025**. I checked amendments for Policy 8C; the amendment tool identified **8C itself as the authoritative current document** and returned no amendments. Citation: [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment).

### 1. Entrance criteria
A beneficiary must meet these entrance criteria:

- Have a **current DSM-5 diagnosis**.
- Present with **behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment** consistent with and associated with the current diagnosis.
- If a **higher level of care is indicated but unavailable**, or the beneficiary is **refusing that service**, outpatient services may be provided until the higher level of care is available or to support the beneficiary in participating in that higher level of care.
- Be **capable of developing skills** to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions.
- There must be **no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective**, based on North Carolina community practice standards.  
  Source: Policy 8C, § 3.2.1.1, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment).

### 2. Continued service criteria
For continued services, the policy requires:

- **Any one** of the following:
  - The desired outcome or level of functioning has **not been restored, improved, or sustained** over the timeframe outlined in the beneficiary’s treatment plan;
  - The beneficiary **continues to be at risk for relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history; **or**
  - The **functional gains are tenuous**.

- And, in addition, **any one** of the following:
  - The beneficiary has **achieved current treatment plan goals, and additional goals are indicated** as evidenced by documented symptoms; **or**
  - The beneficiary is **making satisfactory progress toward meeting goals** and there is documentation that supports that.

Source: Policy 8C, § 3.2.1.2, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment).

> Note: the retrieved text for § 3.2.1.2 appears truncated at the end of the final sentence, so I can verify the criteria above exactly as stated, but I cannot verify whether the section continues with additional words after “supports that.”

### 3. Discharge criteria
A beneficiary meets discharge criteria when:

- The beneficiary’s **level of functioning has improved** with respect to the goals outlined in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary or legally responsible person **no longer wishes to receive these services**; **or**
- Based on the beneficiary’s presentation and **failure to show improvement despite modifications in the treatment plan**, the beneficiary **requires a more appropriate best practice or evidence-based treatment modality** based on North Carolina community practice standards.  
  Source: Policy 8C, § 3.2.1.3, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment).

## Short version
- **Entrance:** diagnosis + functional impairment + outpatient level appropriate/effective.
- **Continued services:** unresolved symptoms/risk or tenuous gains, plus either new goals are indicated or the person is making satisfactory progress.
- **Discharge:** goals/functioning improved, beneficiary wants to stop, or a different treatment modality is more appropriate.

per_question.question: How does the EPSDT special provision affect coverage for outpatient therapy services, and what ordering practitioner requirements apply to beneficiaries under 21?
per_question.agent_answer:
I found the main current policy: Clinical Coverage Policy 10A (effective 2/1/2025), and I checked amendments—none were returned, so 10A is the current authoritative document. Next I’m pulling the full text of the specific EPSDT and ordering-practitioner sections, plus nearby context on visit limits, so I can answer how EPSDT changes therapy coverage for under-21 beneficiaries and who can order services.## Short answer

For outpatient therapy services under **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A**, the **EPSDT special provision** can allow coverage for a Medicaid beneficiary **under age 21** even when the service would otherwise exceed a policy limitation, but **EPSDT does not waive prior approval requirements**. For those under 21, therapy still must be medically necessary, and the policy excludes services that are **unsafe, ineffective, experimental/investigational, or not medical in nature / not generally recognized as accepted medical practice**. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

The applicable **ordering practitioners** for outpatient therapy services in Policy 10A are:
- **Medical Doctor (MD)**
- **Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)**
- **Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM)**
- **Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)**
- **Physician Assistant (PA)**
- **Nurse Practitioner (NP)**  
[[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

## How EPSDT affects outpatient therapy coverage

Policy 10A includes an **“EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age”** in section **2.2.1**, tied to **42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) / Social Security Act § 1905(r)**. The retrieved text shows that EPSDT does **not** permit coverage for services:
- that are **unsafe**,
- **ineffective**,
- **experimental or investigational**, or
- **not medical in nature** or **not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment**. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

That matters because Policy 10A otherwise imposes explicit visit limits only for **beneficiaries age 21 and older**:
- 30 combined OT/PT habilitative visits per calendar year,
- 30 combined OT/PT rehabilitative visits per calendar year,
- 30 speech therapy habilitative visits per calendar year,
- 30 speech therapy rehabilitative visits per calendar year.  
Section **5.3** is titled **“Visit Limitations Beneficiaries 21 Years of Age and Older.”** [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

So, as applied to beneficiaries **under 21**, EPSDT functions as an exception to policy limitations, but not as a blanket override of all utilization controls.

## Prior approval still applies under EPSDT

Policy 10A expressly says:

> If the service, product, or procedure requires prior approval, the fact that the beneficiary is under 21 years of age does **NOT** eliminate the requirement for prior approval.  
[[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

And the treatment-services requirements also say:

- **A verbal or written order must be obtained before services start**;
- **Prior approval is required prior to the start of treatment services**.  
[[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

## Ordering / order requirements for beneficiaries under 21

For outpatient therapy services under Policy 10A, the policy’s listed **ordering practitioners** are:
- MD
- DO
- DPM
- CNM
- PA
- NP  
Section **3.1.2, Ordering Practitioners**. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

Separate from who may order, the treatment-services section imposes these **order mechanics**:
- a **verbal or written order** is required **before services begin**;
- verbal orders must include the date and signature of the person receiving the order, be recorded in the health record, and be **countersigned by the physician within 60 calendar days**;
- verbal orders are valid for **up to six months** from receipt;
- written orders are valid for **up to six months** from the date of the physician’s signature;
- **backdating is not allowed**.  
[[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

## Bottom line

For a beneficiary **under 21**, EPSDT can support coverage of medically necessary outpatient therapy beyond ordinary policy limits, but:
1. the service still must satisfy EPSDT/medical-necessity boundaries,
2. **prior approval is still required** when the policy requires it, and
3. the service must be ordered by one of the practitioner types listed in **section 3.1.2**.  
[[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

I checked amendments for **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A** and the tool returned no amendments; the policy document identified itself as current with an effective date of **February 1, 2025**.

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
I found the main congregate-setting PCS policy and confirmed its eligibility section. I also checked amendments for every document I’m relying on. Next I’m answering the coverage question directly and distinguishing actual Medicaid coverage from the separate budgeting/manual rule about treating PCS costs in adult care homes as a medical expense for deductible purposes.## Short answer

**Yes — NC Medicaid does cover Personal Care Services (PCS) for some beneficiaries who live in an assisted living-type setting, but only if they meet the specific congregate-setting PCS criteria.**

The controlling policy is **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1**, which applies to PCS **provided in congregate settings** such as certain adult care homes and supervised living/group home settings. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## What the policy says

Under **Policy 3L-1, section 3.2.1**, Medicaid covers PCS for a beneficiary who:

- has the required unmet ADL needs,
- **resides in**:
  - “a congregate facility licensed by the State of North Carolina as an **Adult Care Home (ACH)**,”
  - a combination home, or
  - certain licensed supervised living/group home settings,
- and also meets additional conditions such as medical stability, no other third-party payer, and no available willing informal caregiver during the service hours. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

Under **Policy 3L-1, section 3.3**, Medicaid says it **shall cover** PCS tasks in that setting, including hands-on assistance with qualifying ADLs, certain cueing/supervision tied to hands-on assistance, medication assistance when linked to the condition, help with adaptive devices/DME, and certain delegated tasks. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## If by “assisted living facility” you mean an Adult Care Home

In NC policy terms, the closest category is usually an **Adult Care Home**. For those residents, **PCS can be covered** if the resident meets the functional and other policy requirements in **3L-1**. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Important limits

Coverage is **not automatic just because someone lives in assisted living**. The beneficiary must meet the policy’s clinical and setting-based criteria, including:

- minimum ADL impairment thresholds,
- residence in a qualifying licensed congregate setting,
- medical stability,
- no other responsible payer,
- and no available informal caregiver for those service times. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Related budgeting/manual point

The Medicaid eligibility manual also says that in an adult care home, **room and board is not a medical expense**, but **the cost of personal care services received in an adult care home is a medical expense** that can be counted toward the Medicaid deductible. That supports the distinction that PCS in an adult care home is recognized separately from room and board. The section I found is in **MA-2270**. [MA-2270 LONG TERM CARE NEED AND BUDGETING](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/MA-2270-LTC-Need-and-Budgeting.pdf)

- **MA-2270**: I checked amendments. It has multiple change notices, but the amendment summaries returned were about other sections/tables rather than the adult-care-home PCS statement I relied on. The most recent amendment returned was [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 11-25, CHANGES RELATED TO 2026 COST-OF-LIVING ADJUSTMENT (COLA)](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/CN_11-25-ABD.docx.pdf).

**Yes.** A CAP/DA beneficiary can transfer, and NC Medicaid’s CAP/DA policy expressly governs **“Transfers of Eligible Beneficiaries.”** The policy requires the **CME** to coordinate the transfer so there are **no gaps in services**, and it sets specific steps that must occur before and during the transfer. ## Rules that govern transfers

### 1. Transfers are expressly addressed in CAP/DA policy
Section **3.3, “Transfers of Eligible Beneficiaries,”** says the **CME shall coordinate the transfer to prevent gaps in service provisions**. Before the transfer, the following must be completed:

- determine the anticipated start date of service;
- coordinate a transition plan between provider agencies;
- discuss and plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- initiate transfer of the electronic health record in the CAP Business System;
- arrange a home visit within **five business days** after the beneficiary moves to the new primary residence; and
- coordinate services to begin on the **first date of the transfer**.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

### 2. Special rule for transfers to a different county
For a **CAP/DA beneficiary transferring to a different county**, the policy is more specific:

per_question.question: What is the federal statutory authority for NC's CAP/DA waiver, and what does the state need to demonstrate in its waiver application?

I still need the more specific “what must the state demonstrate” requirements from the supporting documentation and assurances sections, plus I need amendment checks for any NC document I cite.## Federal authority for NC’s CAP/DA waiver

NC’s CAP/DA waiver is a **section 1915(c) home- and community-based services (HCBS) waiver**. The federal statutory source is **Social Security Act § 1915(c)**, which allows the Secretary to waive state-plan requirements so a state may treat certain HCBS as Medicaid “medical assistance” for people who, **but for those services, would require institutional level of care** in a hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID. [Social Security Act — Title XIX (Medicaid)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)

NC policy also identifies CAP/DA as one of North Carolina’s **“1915(c) HCBS waivers.”** See [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 3.2.4 (effective Sept. 1, 2025; I checked amendments and the document is returned as current).

## What the state must demonstrate in the waiver application

The implementing federal regulation is **42 CFR Part 441**, especially **§§ 441.301–441.303**. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

In substance, the state’s waiver request must show:

### 1. Required assurances and supporting documentation
A waiver request must include the **assurances in § 441.302** and the **supporting documentation in § 441.303**. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301(a)(1)

### 2. If applicable, what state-plan requirements it seeks to waive
The request must identify any requested waivers of:
- **statewideness**,
- **comparability**, and
- certain **income/resource rules for medically needy individuals in the community**.  
[42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301(a)(2)

### 3. Cost-neutrality / cost comparison
The state must explain whether it will deny HCBS when it reasonably expects the cost to exceed institutional cost, and it must provide documentation showing that the **average per-capita cost under the waiver will not exceed the average per-capita cost absent the waiver**. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) §§ 441.301(a)(3), 441.303(f)

### 4. Who may receive services
The application must provide that services are only for people who:
- are **not inpatients** of a hospital, NF, or ICF/IID, and
- whom the state determines **would otherwise require** that Medicaid-covered institutional level of care.  
[42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301(b)(1)

### 5. Person-centered plan of care
The application must provide that services are delivered under a **written person-centered service plan** approved by the Medicaid agency, and it must describe:
- who develops the plan,
- the person-centered planning process,
- informed choice,
- conflict-of-interest protections,
- and the person-centered service plan requirements.  
[42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301(b)(1), (b)(2), (c)(1)–(2)

### 6. Target group and services
The state must describe:
- the **target group(s)** to be served,
- the **services** to be furnished, with each service separately defined,
- and limit the waiver to one or more permitted target groups, including **aged or disabled** individuals.  
[42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301(b)(3), (4), (6)

### 7. Evaluation and reevaluation process
The state must submit its plan for:
- evaluating and reevaluating beneficiaries,
- who performs those evaluations,
- the evaluation form,
- written documentation,
- and regular reevaluations of need.  
[42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.303(c)

### 8. Choice between institutional and HCBS options
The state must describe how it will inform eligible beneficiaries of feasible alternatives and allow them to choose between **institutional services** and **HCBS**. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.303(d)

### 9. Health and welfare safeguards
The state must assure CMS that it has safeguards to protect beneficiaries’ **health and welfare**, including:
- provider standards,
- compliance with state licensure/certification,
- HCBS settings compliance,
- and incident-management systems.  
[42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.302(a)

### 10. Financial accountability
The state must assure **financial accountability** and describe the records and information it will maintain to support that accountability. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) §§ 441.302(b), 441.303(b)

### 11. Enrollment cap / unduplicated participants
The state must state the number of **unduplicated beneficiaries** it intends to serve each year; that number becomes the waiver limit unless CMS approves an amendment. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.303(f)(6)

## Bottom line

For NC’s CAP/DA waiver, the federal legal authority is **Social Security Act § 1915(c)**, implemented through **42 CFR Part 441**. In its waiver application, North Carolina must demonstrate to CMS, at minimum, that:

- the waiver serves people who would otherwise need institutional care,
- the waiver includes required person-centered planning and service definitions,
- beneficiaries are protected through health-and-welfare safeguards,
- beneficiaries have a choice between institutional and community services,
- the program is financially accountable,
- and the waiver is **cost-neutral** on the required federal per-capita expenditure basis.

per_question.question: How many days of therapeutic leave from a nursing facility does NC Medicaid allow per year, and what conditions must be met?

NC Medicaid allows **up to 60 days of therapeutic leave per calendar year** for a Medicaid-eligible resident occupying a reimbursed nursing facility bed. Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 2B-1, § 5.8**, the leave must meet these conditions:

- Medicaid does **not** apply therapeutic leave when the resident is away **to receive inpatient or nursing services elsewhere, or at a different level of care in the same facility, if Medicaid is paying for those services**.
- **Ambulance transportation** to the therapeutic leave site is **not reimbursed** because it is not considered an emergency. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)] § 5.8

The NC Medicaid state plan contains substantially the same rule: **60 days per calendar year**, physician order, plan-of-care documentation, bed reservation, and **15-day consecutive limit without approval**. ### Bottom line
For a nursing facility resident, the rule is:

- **60 days total per year**
- **15 consecutive days max without NC Medicaid approval**
- Must be **therapeutic**, **physician-ordered**, and **documented in the care plan and record**.

per_question.question: What are the specific criteria for NC Medicaid coverage of CAR-T cell therapy?
per_question.agent_answer:
I found the current NC Medicaid clinical policy specifically for CAR-T cell therapy and confirmed through the amendments tool that the authoritative document is the current 04/01/2025 version. I also pulled the key coverage, noncoverage, and prior-authorization documentation sections. Next I’ll summarize the actual coverage criteria and separate them from the PA submission requirements.## NC Medicaid coverage criteria for CAR-T cell therapy

NC Medicaid has a dedicated current policy for this: **Clinical Coverage Policy 11A-17, CAR-T Cell Therapy**, effective **April 1, 2025**. I checked for amendments, and the tool returned this document as the **current authoritative version** with no separate amending change notice identified in the amendment tool results. [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

### A. General medical-necessity criteria
To be covered, the service must meet NC Medicaid’s general coverage standards:

- be **individualized, specific, and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis**, and **not in excess of the beneficiary’s needs**;
- be able to be **safely furnished**; and
- have **no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide**;
- and not be furnished primarily for the convenience of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider.  
[Citation: Clinical Coverage Policy 11A-17, § 3.1, effective 04/01/2025](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

### B. CAR-T-specific coverage criteria
NC Medicaid specifically covers CAR-T cell therapy only when all of the following are met:

- the **CAR-T therapy has received FDA approval**;
- it is administered **according to FDA-approved guidelines** for:
  - indications and usage,
  - dosage and administration,
  - dosage forms and strengths, and
  - warnings and precautions;
- it is administered at a **certified or authorized treatment center**; and
- **if the therapy is subject to a REMS program**, the treatment center must be **enrolled in that REMS**, and providers must be **trained in management of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurologic toxicities**.  
[Citation: Clinical Coverage Policy 11A-17, § 3.2.1, effective 04/01/2025](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## When NC Medicaid will not cover it
The same policy says CAR-T therapy is **not covered** if, among other things:

- the therapy is **not FDA approved**;
- it is administered **outside FDA guidelines** for indications/usage, dosage/administration, or dosage forms/strengths;
- for a therapy requiring REMS, it is given at a facility **not enrolled in that therapy’s REMS**;
- it is a **repeat treatment** in a beneficiary who has previously received another CAR-T therapy;
- the beneficiary’s **psychosocial history limits ability to comply** with pre- and post-infusion care; or
- there is current beneficiary or caretaker **noncompliance** making adherence to a disciplined medical regimen improbable.  
[Citation: Clinical Coverage Policy 11A-17, § 4.2.1, effective 04/01/2025](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

More generally, NC Medicaid also does not cover the service if the beneficiary does not meet Section 3 criteria, if the service duplicates another provider’s service, or if it is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**.  
[Citation: Clinical Coverage Policy 11A-17, § 4.1, effective 04/01/2025](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## Prior authorization documentation required
Although this is not the same thing as the substantive coverage standard, NC Medicaid also requires specific documentation for approval, including:

- a **letter of medical necessity** signed by the attending physician documenting prior chemotherapy regimens and dates, clinical and social history, and indications for CAR-T treatment;
- verification that the facility is a **qualified/authorized treatment center** for the requested CAR-T product;
- recent **HIV and hepatitis serologies**;
- diagnostic and procedure results, including **bone marrow biopsy** not more than six months old;
- other diagnostic tests if requested; and
- a **complete psychological and social evaluation**, including:
  - medical compliance,
  - support network,
  - post-treatment care plan with primary and secondary care providers, and
  - history of mental health issues, substance use, or legal issues.  
[Citation: Clinical Coverage Policy 11A-17, § 5.2.2, effective 04/01/2025](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## Bottom line
NC Medicaid does **not** list fixed disease-by-disease criteria in this policy section. Instead, the policy ties coverage to:

1. **general medical necessity**,  
2. **FDA approval of the specific CAR-T product**,  
3. use **within the FDA-approved labeling/guidelines**, and  
4. administration at a **qualified treatment center**, including **REMS compliance** when required.  

The policy also makes psychosocial suitability and ability to comply with pre/post-infusion care relevant, because those factors appear in the noncoverage and prior-authorization sections. [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

per_question.question: Until what age should physicians provide fluoride varnish applications for Medicaid beneficiaries, and what oral screening requirements apply?
per_question.agent_answer:

The billing sections also state the service is **limited to beneficiaries under 3½ years of age**, **allowed once every 60 calendar days**, and **limited to six times before the child reaches 3½**. ### Oral screening requirements
NC Medicaid’s physician fluoride varnish policy requires:

- **Early caries screening**
- **Detection of notable findings**—described as obvious pathology of hard and soft tissues in the oral cavity—**using a dental mirror and directed light**
- **Counseling and educational materials** on good oral hygiene practices and nutrition for children
- **Prescribing a fluoride supplement, if indicated**
- **Application of fluoride varnish to all erupted primary teeth**

The policy also requires documentation in the beneficiary’s health record of:

- **an oral evaluation and any notable findings**
- **preventive oral health and dietary counseling with the primary caregiver**
- **application of fluoride varnish**
- **referral to a dentist, if appropriate**

[Physician Fluoride Varnish Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment), § 7.2.

The oral evaluation code **D0145**:
- is for a patient under three years of age and counseling with the primary caregiver,
- includes early caries screening, evaluation of caries susceptibility, and recording of notable findings,
- **must be billed with D1206**.

The fluoride varnish code **D1206**:
- **must be billed with D0145**.

[Physician Fluoride Varnish Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment), §§ 5.3.1, 5.3.2.

per_question.question: Can an NC Innovations waiver participant request services that exceed their individual base budget, and what happens if they believe their needs cannot be met within the budget?
per_question.agent_answer:
I found the key NC Innovations budget language in Attachment F of Policy 8-P, and I checked amendments for Policy 8-P; the tool shows no amendments and treats 8-P as the current authoritative document. Next I’m pulling the adjacent budget sections so I can explain what happens when needs exceed the base budget and whether there is any formal review/change process.The adjacent headings didn’t yield usable body text in this corpus, but the core rule is clear: the base budget is not a binding cap, medically necessary services can be requested above it, and denials must include appeal information. I’m doing one more targeted search for any text about grievances, appeals, or review tied specifically to base budgets or authorization denials.## Short answer

**Yes.** An NC Innovations participant **may request services that cost more than their individual base budget** if they believe their needs cannot be met within that budget. Under NC Medicaid policy, the **base budget and SIS results are only guidelines, not a binding cap**. If the LME/MCO determines the requested services are **medically necessary**, they **must be authorized regardless of the base budget**. If the request is denied, the participant must be told the reasons and **how to appeal**, and the policy also says they must be told **how to file a grievance regarding the base budget**. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment), effective 11/1/2016, current per amendment check)

## What the policy says

In Attachment F of **Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P**, NC Medicaid states that a beneficiary:

- “**may request services that cost in excess of his or her base budget** if he or she believes his or her needs cannot be met within his or her base budget”; and
- “**the results of the SIS and the base budget are guidelines that do not constitute a binding limit** on the amount of services that may be requested or authorized, and if the LME/MCO determines services to be **medically necessary**, they will be authorized, **regardless of the base budget**.” ([Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment), Attachment F, “Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes,” effective 11/1/2016, current per amendment check)

That same section says:

- if a request for authorization is denied, the LME/MCO will notify the individual of the reasons and **how to appeal**; and
- the individual must also be informed **how to file a grievance regarding the base budget**. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment), Attachment F, “Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes,” effective 11/1/2016, current per amendment check)

## What happens in practice if needs cannot be met within budget

Based on the policy text I retrieved, the process is:

1. **The participant can ask for services above the base budget.**
2. The **LME/MCO reviews medical necessity**.
3. If the services are found medically necessary, they **can be approved even if they exceed the base budget**.
4. If denied, the participant must receive:
   - the **reasons for the denial**,
   - instructions on **how to appeal**, and
   - information on **how to file a grievance regarding the base budget**. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment), Attachment F, “Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes,” effective 11/1/2016, current per amendment check)

Also, when an ISP is approved, the beneficiary or guardian must get **written notice and a copy of the approved ISP, including the Individual Budget**. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment), § 5.4.5, effective 11/1/2016, current per amendment check)

## Federal backdrop

Federal HCBS waiver rules require a **person-centered service plan** and say the individual leads the planning process, is offered informed choices, and must have a method to request plan updates as needed. ([42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.301, current per amendment check)

I did **not** retrieve a federal section here that directly says NC must approve every over-budget request; the direct authority for that point in this answer is the NC Innovations policy itself. The federal rule is helpful background because it supports individualized, person-centered planning.

## Bottom line

A participant is **not stuck with the base budget as an absolute ceiling**. If they believe their needs cannot be met within it, they can **request more services**, and those services may be approved if the LME/MCO finds them **medically necessary**. If the request is denied, they should receive written reasons plus information about **appeal rights** and **grievance rights**.

per_question.question: What are the certification requirements for HIV case management providers under NC Medicaid, and under what conditions can a provider be decertified?
per_question.agent_answer:
I found the key governing document: Clinical Coverage Policy 12B has explicit sections on certification, recertification, and decertification, and there are no retrieved amendments superseding the current 12B version. Next I’m pulling the full text of the certification/decertification sections and a few related qualification sections so I can answer precisely.I now have the full 12B certification, recertification, and decertification text, plus the staff qualification sections. The answer is driven mainly by §§ 6.2.1, 6.2.4, and 6.2.5 of Policy 12B, with the recertification checklist adding detail on the kinds of documents DHHS expects.## HIV case management provider certification requirements under NC Medicaid

Under **NC Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy 12B**, an HIV case management provider must meet these certification requirements:

- Have **a documented successful record of 3 years of providing or managing HIV Case Management programs**.
- Ensure services are provided by **qualified case managers** meeting the standards in Policy 12B § 6.1.1, § 6.1.2, and § 6.1.3.
- Ensure HIV case management is supervised by **qualified supervisors** meeting § 6.1.4 and § 6.1.5.
- **Enroll each physical site** with NC Medicaid as an HIV Case Management provider.
- Meet **applicable state and federal Medicaid participation laws**.
- **Maintain certification** as a qualified HIV case management provider.
- Demonstrate compliance with **initial and ongoing certification processes**.
- Demonstrate compliance with **monitoring and evaluation of case management records through a quality improvement plan**.
- Allow **NC Medicaid or its DHHS-designated contractor** to review beneficiary records and inspect agency operations and financial records.
- Notify NC Medicaid or its contractor of proposed business changes—such as owner/name/address/phone changes or dissolution plans—**within 30 calendar days of the proposed change and no later than 5 business days after the actual change**.
- **Within 1 year of Medicaid enrollment**, achieve national accreditation from one of the designated accrediting bodies: **ACHC, CARF, CHAP, COA, PHAB, The Joint Commission, or URAC**.  
  Source: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment) (Policy 12B, § 6.2.1; effective 2020-01-15; no amendments retrieved)

### Staff qualification requirements tied to certification
Policy 12B also ties provider certification to staff credentials.

**Case managers** must meet one of several education/experience pathways, including certain human-services degrees or specified licensure plus relevant experience.  
Source: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment) (Policy 12B, § 6.1.1; effective 2020-01-15; no amendments retrieved)

**Supervisors** must likewise meet specified degree/licensure and experience combinations.  
Source: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment) (Policy 12B, § 6.1.4; effective 2020-01-15; no amendments retrieved)

**Training** for case managers and supervisors must cover HIV information, prevention, scope of work, core components of HIV case management, ethics, system-of-care responsibilities, and documentation requirements.  
Source: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment) (Policy 12B, § 6.1.7.1; effective 2020-01-15; no amendments retrieved)

### Recertification requirements
For recertification, the provider must:

- Submit a **complete and signed Recertification Application** within **60 calendar days of receipt**;
- Submit copies of items from the initial certification package that have changed;
- Submit copies of **all HIV case manager and supervisor credentials**;
- Submit **annual summaries of quality improvement activities**, including outcome metrics; and
- Undergo a **recertification on-site visit**, including record and business documentation review if needed.  
  Source: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment) (Policy 12B, § 6.2.4; effective 2020-01-15; no amendments retrieved)

The DHHS recertification checklist also shows DHHS expects documentation such as agency demographics, staffing lists, counties served, operating hours, emergency after-hours plan, accreditation information, quality assurance materials, organizational chart, community resources, staff credentials, and signed compliance attestations.  
Source: [dma-3157 HIV Case Management Provider Recertification Application Checklist](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/dma-3157.pdf) (current; no amendments retrieved)

---

## When can an HIV case management provider be decertified?

Under **Policy 12B § 6.2.5**, a provider can be decertified for any of the following:

- **Failure to provide core service components**
- **Fraudulent billing practices**
- **Owner conviction of a felony**
- Failure to **develop, submit, and implement a written plan of correction** for unmet program requirements cited by NC Medicaid or its contractor, including failure to make recommended corrections, **within 30 calendar days**
- **Falsification of records**
- **Violation of beneficiary confidentiality**
- Employment of staff who **do not meet the criteria in § 6.1**
- Failure of staff to complete required **mandatory basic training within 90 days of employment**
- Failure of staff to obtain required **continuing education units (CEUs)**
- Failure to provide case management staff with **supervision sufficient to meet beneficiaries’ needs**
- Failure to submit required documentation within the time frame required by the policy, NC Medicaid, or its contractor
- Failure to provide documentation sufficient to support billing, as required by **§ 7.5**
- Failure to **implement and enforce a quality improvement program**
- Failure to timely notify NC Medicaid or its contractor of changes in agency name, director/ownership, address, or phone, resulting in inability to contact the provider
- Failure to comply with **applicable federal and state laws, regulations, the state reimbursement plan, and Medicaid policies**
- Failure to enroll any beneficiaries **within 4 months of certification**
- Failure to **achieve or maintain certification requirements** under § 6.2  
  Source: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment) (Policy 12B, § 6.2.5; effective 2020-01-15; no amendments retrieved)

## Bottom line
A provider must show organizational experience, qualified staff and supervision, site-specific Medicaid enrollment, compliance systems, quality improvement, records access, change reporting, and accreditation within 1 year. A provider can be decertified for fraud, records/confidentiality violations, unqualified or untrained staff, inadequate supervision or documentation, failure to correct deficiencies, broader legal noncompliance, or failure to maintain certification standards.
